name: Göbekli Tepe
desc: A hill of T-shaped limestone pillars carved with foxes, vultures and scorpions, raised by hunter-gatherers around 9600 BC — six thousand years before Stonehenge. It rewrote the story of when humans started building monuments, and it is still mostly underground.
season: Apr–May and Oct–Nov — the shelter traps heat and July is punishing
tip: Go at opening or in the last hour; the walkway is a fixed one-way loop and a tour group ahead of you means you see backs of heads for forty minutes.
todo: Enclosure D's two central pillars with carved arms
The fox and the vulture reliefs
Şanlıurfa museum after, for the finds
rev: Visitors call it genuinely moving once the age sinks in, but many arrive expecting a vast site and find a modest sheltered dig — going without reading up first is the commonest disappointment.
onward: Şanlıurfa GAP (GNY), then 40 min by car; minibuses run from Urfa's Balıklıgöl in season

name: Karahan Tepe
desc: Göbekli Tepe's contemporary and, to many archaeologists, the more startling site: a room with eleven phallic pillars rising from bedrock and a human head carved into the rock wall, watching. It opened to visitors recently and still feels like a working dig rather than an attraction.
tip: Combine it with Göbekli Tepe in one day but do Karahan first — after the crowds and walkways of Göbekli it feels twice as raw.
todo: The carved head emerging from the wall
The long view over the Tektek plateau
rev: Those who make the drive rate it above Göbekli Tepe for atmosphere, but the road is rough, there is almost no shade or infrastructure, and excavation can close sections without notice.
onward: Şanlıurfa GAP (GNY), then about 1h15 east by car — there is no public transport, so hire or a driver

name: Balıklıgöl
desc: Two rectangular pools of sacred carp below the citadel rock, where tradition says Abraham was thrown into a fire that turned to water. Families feed the fish, pilgrims pray at the Halil-ür Rahman mosque, and the whole thing works as the city's living room.
season: Year-round — evenings from Apr to Oct, when the courtyards fill
tip: Climb the citadel steps at sunset for the view down over both pools, then come back through the rose garden when the lights come on.
todo: Feed the carp at Halil-ür Rahman
The Cave of Abraham beside the mosque
rev: Reviewers love the atmosphere and the free entry, though some find the commercial fish-food sellers pushy and the site far busier on Fridays and religious holidays.
onward: Şanlıurfa GAP (GNY), 45 min by shuttle or taxi into the centre; everything old is then walkable

name: Şanlıurfa Covered Bazaar
desc: A working Ottoman bazaar rather than a souvenir one: felt-makers, coppersmiths hammering, sacks of isot pepper, and the Gümrük Han courtyard where old men play backgammon under a vine with tea coming every ten minutes.
season: Year-round — mornings; closed Sunday in parts
tip: Sit in Gümrük Han for a menengiç coffee, then buy isot pepper by weight from a spice seller rather than a pre-packed tourist box.
todo: Tea in the Gümrük Han courtyard
Buy isot pepper and Urfa peanuts
rev: Consistently the highlight for people who came for the archaeology, though the alleys are confusing, and a few visitors report being steered toward a relative's shop by over-helpful guides.
onward: Şanlıurfa GAP (GNY), 45 min to the centre; the bazaar is a five-minute walk from Balıklıgöl

name: Harran
desc: Conical mud-brick beehive houses on a plain that has been farmed for five thousand years, beside the ruins of one of the world's oldest universities and a moon-god temple. The domes are built without timber and stay startlingly cool inside.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — the plain hits 45 °C in summer
tip: The beehive houses in the village centre are a paid tourist set-up; walk five minutes out to see families still living in the real ones.
todo: Inside a beehive house, for the cool
The ruined Grand Mosque and its minaret
The castle mound at the edge of the village
rev: The architecture is genuinely unique and the setting stark and memorable, but visitors regularly mention children asking for money and an entrance experience that feels staged.
entry: ₺100 (≈€2.20) for the house complex · ruins free
onward: Şanlıurfa GAP (GNY), then 1h south by car; minibuses leave Urfa's otogar hourly

name: Soğmatar
desc: A hill sanctuary of the Sabians, who worshipped the sun, moon and five planets here in the second century. Rock-cut reliefs of robed figures stare out of a basalt outcrop above a village where nothing much has changed, and you will usually have it alone.
tip: Find the village muhtar or the boy with the key for the underground Pognon cave, which holds the best-preserved reliefs and is otherwise locked.
todo: The seven planet-shrines around the village
rev: Travellers who reach it describe it as the most atmospheric site in the region, but there is no signage, no ticket office and no shade, and the last few kilometres of road are rough.
entry: Free · a tip to whoever unlocks the cave is customary
onward: Şanlıurfa GAP (GNY), then about 1h30 by car via Harran — you need your own vehicle

name: Şuayb City
desc: A Roman town half-collapsed into the limestone it was cut from: doorframes, rock chambers and cisterns spread over a hillside, with local families still using some of the caves as animal shelters. Named for the prophet Shuayb, whose supposed cave draws pilgrims.
tip: Pair it with Soğmatar 15 km away — the two together make the best half-day in the Tektek hills, and one drive covers both.
todo: The cisterns cut into the rock
rev: Visitors like the sense of discovery and the complete absence of crowds, but note there is no interpretation whatsoever and the ruins are unstable in places.
onward: Şanlıurfa GAP (GNY), then about 1h15 by car; combine with Soğmatar and Harran in one loop

name: Han el-Ba'rur
desc: A square Ayyubid caravanserai from 1216 standing alone on the Tektek plateau, its stone arches and camel stalls intact enough that you can read the building at a glance. Nothing else is visible in any direction.
tip: It is unlocked and unstaffed — go in the last hour of light, when the low sun comes through the arches and the plateau turns orange.
todo: The plateau view from the roofline
rev: A favourite of people doing the Tektek loop for its isolation and photogenic arches, though it takes about fifteen minutes to see and is not worth a dedicated trip.
onward: Şanlıurfa GAP (GNY), then 1h20 by car on the Soğmatar–Şuayb loop

name: Birecik and the Bald Ibis
desc: The last semi-wild colony of northern bald ibis in the Middle East, a bird that nearly vanished entirely, kept going on cliffs above the Euphrates at Birecik. The town itself is a pistachio-and-tea river stop with a Crusader castle.
season: Mar–Jul, when the birds are at the colony; they are penned over winter
tip: Come in the morning when the birds are active on the cliff ledges, and ask at the station rather than trying to spot them from the road.
rev: Birdwatchers rate the colony as unmissable, though casual visitors sometimes find the enclosure setting more zoo than wilderness, and the station keeps irregular hours.
entry: Free or a nominal fee · check opening before travelling
onward: Şanlıurfa GAP (GNY) or Gaziantep (GZT), each about 1h15 by car; frequent buses on the Antep–Urfa road

name: Atatürk Dam
desc: One of the largest dams on earth, holding back an inland sea of Euphrates water that turned the dry southeast green and drowned a good deal of history doing it. The scale from the viewing terrace is genuinely hard to process.
tip: The best view is not the dam wall but the road along the reservoir toward Siverek, where the water fills whole valleys between bare hills.
todo: The viewing terrace over the wall
rev: Impressive as engineering and good for a break on a long drive, but there is little to actually do, security restricts photography near the wall, and summer heat off the water is fierce.
entry: Free · photography restricted at the dam itself
onward: Şanlıurfa GAP (GNY), then about 1h15 north by car on the Bozova road

name: Halfeti
desc: A stone town half-drowned by the Birecik dam, where boats glide over submerged streets and a minaret rises straight out of green water. The famous near-black roses grow in the surviving upper gardens.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the roses flower in spring
tip: Take the boat from Halfeti rather than Rumkale side, go late afternoon, and ask the boatman to cut the engine over the sunken village.
todo: The black roses in the upper gardens
rev: The boat trip is widely called magical, but the village itself has become heavily commercialised, boatmen quote wildly different prices, and weekends bring domestic tour buses in numbers.
entry: Free · boat trips ₺300–600 (≈€6–13) per person depending on route
onward: Gaziantep (GZT) or Şanlıurfa GAP (GNY), each about 1h30 by car; buses run from Birecik

name: Rumkale
desc: A fortress on a rock spur where the Merzimen stream meets the Euphrates, cut off on three sides by water since the dam rose. Armenian, Byzantine and Islamic layers pile on top of each other, reachable only by boat.
tip: Boats leave from both Halfeti and Savaşan; the Savaşan side is cheaper and quieter, and you get the sunken-village view on the way.
todo: The rock-cut well shaft to the river
The confluence view from the walls
rev: The approach by water is the best part and reviewers agree it is worth the trip, though the site itself is unrestored, slippery, and boat operators sometimes allow only a short stop.
onward: Gaziantep (GZT), then 1h30 by car to Halfeti or Savaşan, then boat

name: Zeugma Mosaic Museum
desc: The largest mosaic museum in the world, built to hold what was rescued from Zeugma before the Euphrates rose over it. The Gypsy Girl fragment — a pair of eyes that follow you across a darkened room — is the reason most people come, and it earns it.
season: Year-round — indoors and air-conditioned, which matters here
tip: Do the museum in the afternoon when the light outside is unbearable, and see the Gypsy Girl room last so it lands properly.
near: Zeugma Mozaik Müzesi, Şehitkamil, Gaziantep, Türkiye
todo: The Gypsy Girl in her dark room
The Mars statue and fountain mosaics
rev: Almost universally praised as world-class and worth a trip to Gaziantep on its own, with the main complaint being that the Gypsy Girl room is small and gets congested with tour groups.
onward: Gaziantep (GZT), 25 min by taxi or tram plus a short walk

name: Gaziantep Castle
desc: A round Roman-then-Byzantine citadel on a mound in the middle of the city, damaged in the 2023 earthquake and partly under restoration. Even from the outside it anchors the old town, with the copper bazaar running off its skirts.
season: Year-round — spring and autumn are pleasant, summer is not
tip: Check whether the castle itself has reopened before planning around it; the circuit of the mound and the bazaar below are the real experience either way.
todo: The walls circuit and city view
The copper bazaar at the foot
Baklava at a house that has been there a century
rev: Visitors value it as the heart of the old city, but many arrive to find sections closed for post-earthquake restoration and note that the interior museum has been shut for extended periods.
entry: Free to circle · interior fee when open, check locally
onward: Gaziantep (GZT), 25 min into the centre; the old town is walkable from there

name: Bakırcılar Bazaar
desc: The coppersmiths' quarter, where the sound arrives before the sight — dozens of workshops beating trays, coffee pots and cauldrons by hand. Around it sit spice stalls, the pistachio wholesalers and some of the best-value food in the country.
season: Year-round — mornings, when the hammering starts
tip: Buy a hand-hammered coffee pot here rather than in Istanbul; the same object costs a fraction and you can watch it being finished.
rev: Food-minded travellers rate the whole quarter as the best market experience in Türkiye, though earthquake damage closed parts of the surrounding hans and some workshops have not returned.
onward: Gaziantep (GZT), 25 min to the centre; the bazaar sits below the castle

name: Emine Göğüş Culinary Museum
desc: A restored 19th-century stone house explaining why Gaziantep is a UNESCO City of Gastronomy: the pepper varieties, the pistachio grades, the forty kinds of kebab and the correct way to layer baklava, laid out room by room.
tip: Do it before you start eating your way round the city rather than after — it changes what you order for the rest of the trip.
near: Emine Göğüş Mutfak Müzesi, Şahinbey, Gaziantep, Türkiye
rev: Small but well judged, and cheap; the recurring criticism is that English labelling is thin and the whole visit takes barely half an hour.
onward: Gaziantep (GZT), 25 min to the centre; a short walk from the castle

name: Zeugma Ancient City
desc: The Hellenistic bridgehead city on the Euphrates whose villas produced the mosaics now in Gaziantep. Much of it lies under the Birecik reservoir; what survives above water is a terraced site of house foundations looking down at the river that took the rest.
tip: See the museum in Gaziantep first — without it the site reads as bare foundations, and with it you can place every mosaic you saw.
todo: The waterline where the city ends
The Euphrates view from the upper terrace
rev: Rewarding for people who care about the story of the rescue dig, but visitors expecting a standing ancient city are routinely underwhelmed by what is left.
onward: Gaziantep (GZT), then 1h east by car via Nizip

name: Yesemek Quarry
desc: The largest known open-air sculpture workshop of the ancient Near East: several hundred half-finished Hittite lions, sphinxes and mountain gods lying on a hillside exactly where the carvers abandoned them nearly three thousand years ago.
tip: Walk the whole upper slope, not just the marked path — the unfinished lions above the treeline are the ones that make the place.
todo: Sphinx blocks still attached to bedrock
rev: Archaeology enthusiasts find it extraordinary and are usually alone there, though the site is exposed, poorly signposted, and a long detour from anywhere else.
onward: Gaziantep (GZT), then about 1h30 southwest by car via İslahiye

name: Dülük and Keber Tepe
desc: Ancient Doliche, home of the cult of Jupiter Dolichenus that spread to every corner of the Roman empire, with rock-cut Mithraeum chambers and a quarried hillside just north of Gaziantep. Locals come for the pine woods and picnics rather than the archaeology.
tip: The Mithraeum caves are the point and they are easy to walk past; ask for the Mithras mağarası, not the picnic area.
rev: A pleasant short trip out of the city and free, but the ancient remains are scattered and unexplained, and weekends bring heavy picnic traffic.
onward: Gaziantep (GZT), then 25 min north by car

name: Mount Nemrut
desc: A first-century BC king built his own tomb on a 2,150 m summit and ringed it with colossal seated gods, then piled a cone of broken stone over the burial. Earthquakes toppled the heads, which now sit on the ground staring past you at the sunrise.
season: Late May–mid Oct — the summit road is closed by snow the rest of the year
tip: Sunrise means leaving Kahta around 03:00 and it is genuinely cold at the top even in August; sunset is warmer, emptier and lights the east terrace better.
todo: The toppled heads of Zeus and Antiochus
rev: Repeatedly described as one of the great sights of Türkiye, with the caveats that the final climb is a steep 600 m on loose stone, sunrise is crowded and freezing, and the road closes with early snow.
onward: Adıyaman (ADF), then about 2h by car to the summit car park via Kahta; tours run from Kahta and Malatya

name: Arsameia on the Nymphaios
desc: The Commagene summer capital below Nemrut, where a relief shows King Mithridates shaking hands with Heracles, and a long tunnel drops into the hillside toward a cult chamber nobody has fully explained.
tip: Bring a torch for the tunnel; it goes further than you expect and there is no lighting past the first few metres.
rev: A strong companion to Nemrut and usually quiet, though it is a hot uphill walk with almost no shade and the tunnel is closed off after heavy rain.
onward: Adıyaman (ADF), then 1h15 by car; every Nemrut tour from Kahta stops here

name: Cendere Bridge
desc: A Roman bridge from around AD 200 still carrying its single 30-metre arch over the Cendere gorge, with three of its four honorific columns standing. It served traffic until recently and looks barely touched.
tip: Walk down to the riverbed on the south side for the view that shows the whole arch — from the road you only see the deck.
todo: The arch from the riverbed below
rev: A quick, free and photogenic stop that everyone on the Nemrut circuit enjoys, though it is genuinely a ten-minute visit and the riverbank collects litter.
onward: Adıyaman (ADF), then about 1h by car on the Kahta–Nemrut road

name: Karakuş Tumulus
desc: A burial mound for the women of the Commagene royal house, marked by tall columns topped with an eagle, a lion and a relief of a handshake farewell. It stands alone above the Euphrates plain and catches extraordinary evening light.
tip: It is the best sunset spot on the Nemrut circuit and almost nobody stops — save it for last on the way back to Kahta.
todo: The eagle column against the sky
rev: Photographers rate it highly for the light and emptiness, but there is little to do beyond looking, and it is skipped by some tours.
onward: Adıyaman (ADF), then 40 min by car toward Kahta

name: Perre Ancient City
desc: A Commagene and Roman necropolis cut straight into the rock at the edge of Adıyaman, with chamber tombs, a monumental fountain still running, and carved facades you can walk into. It sits within the modern town, which makes the scale of it stranger.
tip: Go early or late; the rock faces bake by mid-morning and the chambers are the only shade for a kilometre.
rev: Good value and easy to reach from town, though the site is small and visitors note that some tombs are fenced off and the surroundings are built up.
onward: Adıyaman (ADF), then 20 min by taxi — it is on the edge of the city

name: Besni Old Town
desc: An abandoned hillside town of stone houses and a ruined castle, evacuated after landslides and now slowly being consolidated as an open-air site. Empty streets, collapsed vaults and long views over the Besni plain.
tip: The new town below is where the famous Besni grapes and its pekmez come from — buy some at a roadside stall on the way out.
todo: The ruined castle above the old town
Besni grapes and pekmez in the new town
rev: Atmospheric and completely uncommercial, but it is a genuine ruin field with unstable buildings, minimal signage and no facilities.
onward: Adıyaman (ADF), then 50 min southwest by car

name: Mardin Old Town
desc: A city of honey-coloured limestone stacked in terraces down a hillside, with the Mesopotamian plain running flat to the horizon below. Arabic, Kurdish, Turkish and Syriac have all shaped it, and the stone carving on ordinary doorways is extraordinary.
season: Apr–May and Sep–Nov — July and August are brutal
tip: Stay in the old town, not the new city below, and walk the lower lane rather than the main street — the views under the arches are what people remember.
todo: The Zinciriye madrasa terrace at sunset
Carved doorways along the lower lanes
Coffee with cardamom in a stone courtyard
rev: Widely called the most beautiful town in Türkiye, with the honest caveats that it is steep and hard on the knees, the main street is now solidly souvenir shops, and it is packed at holidays.
onward: Mardin (MQM), then 25 min by car up to the old town; the airport is unusually close

name: Deyrulzafaran Monastery
desc: The Saffron Monastery, seat of the Syriac Orthodox patriarchate for six centuries, built over a temple where the sun was worshipped. Services are still held in Aramaic, and the underground chamber below the church is older than everything above it.
season: Mar–Nov — closed to visitors during some services
tip: Time your visit for a service if you can; hearing Aramaic sung in the church is worth more than the guided walk-through.
rev: Visitors find it beautiful and still living rather than museum-like, though the compulsory guided format is rushed and photography is restricted inside the church.
onward: Mardin (MQM), then 30 min by car — 6 km east of the old town

name: Kasımiye Madrasa
desc: A 15th-century madrasa whose courtyard pool is cut in the shape of a life: a channel that narrows and widens from birth to death. From its terrace the whole Mesopotamian plain opens out, which is the single best view in Mardin.
tip: Come 45 minutes before sunset, when the stone goes gold and the plain below turns purple; it is far less crowded than the Zinciriye.
todo: The terrace view over the plain
rev: Frequently rated better than the more famous Zinciriye for both architecture and calm, though it is a stiff walk up from the main street and closes earlier than people expect.
onward: Mardin (MQM), 25 min by car, then a steep uphill walk from the main street

name: Midyat
desc: The stone heart of the Tur Abdin plateau, where Syriac silversmiths still make telkari filigree and the old quarter of Estel is a maze of carved limestone courtyards. Quieter and less polished than Mardin, and better for it.
tip: Sleep here rather than day-tripping — the guesthouses in old stone konaks are the whole point, and the town empties beautifully after dark.
rev: Travellers consistently prefer Midyat's atmosphere to Mardin's commerce, though there is less to formally see, and a popular Turkish TV series has brought weekend crowds to one particular mansion.
entry: Free · guesthouse courtyards usually welcome visitors for tea
onward: Mardin (MQM), then 1h east by car; regular minibuses from Mardin otogar

name: Mor Gabriel Monastery
desc: Founded in 397, the oldest working Syriac Orthodox monastery in the world, still home to a small community on the bare Tur Abdin plateau. The mosaic in the main church was a gift from a Byzantine emperor.
season: Mar–Nov — visiting hours are limited and strictly kept
tip: Check the visiting window before you drive out; it opens for only a couple of hours in the afternoon and turns people away outside it.
near: Mor Gabriel Manastırı, Midyat, Mardin, Türkiye
todo: The imperial mosaic in the church
The plateau view from the walls
rev: A moving stop for anyone interested in early Christianity, but access is tightly controlled, the visit is short and guided, and modest dress is enforced.
onward: Mardin (MQM), then about 1h15 by car past Midyat

name: Dara Ancient City
desc: A Byzantine frontier fortress town cut into and out of the rock: a vast pillared cistern, a necropolis of rock tombs, and a bone-filled burial chamber, with a modern village living among the ruins.
tip: The great cistern is the reason to come and it is easy to miss — it is down a lane behind the village, not on the main path.
rev: Repeatedly named the surprise of a southeast trip, though signage is poor, the village dogs are assertive, and there is no shade at all.
onward: Mardin (MQM), then 40 min southeast by car

name: Savur
desc: A small stone town spilling down a bluff above a green river valley, often called a miniature Mardin but with orchards instead of a plain below. Almost no tourism, a castle ruin on top and very good breakfasts.
tip: Walk down to the river gardens below the town in the late afternoon — the view back up at the stacked houses is the one worth having.
todo: The castle ruin above the houses
rev: Loved by the few who detour for it and described as Mardin without the crowds, though there is little to actually do and accommodation is limited to a handful of guesthouses.
onward: Mardin (MQM), then 45 min northeast by car; minibuses run from Mardin

name: Nusaybin and Mor Yakup
desc: Ancient Nisibis on the Syrian border, where the fourth-century church of Mor Yakup holds one of the oldest surviving Christian crypts anywhere, and a Roman bridge and city wall fragments surface between modern streets.
tip: The crypt and its carved capitals are the point; ask at the site office, as the lower chamber is often locked between visitors.
rev: Historically significant and rarely visited, though the border-town setting is heavily policed, the site is fragmentary, and travellers should check current advisories before going.
onward: Mardin (MQM), then 1h south by car; check border-region advisories before travelling

name: Diyarbakır City Walls
desc: Nearly six kilometres of black basalt wall, second in length only to the Great Wall, wrapped around the old city since Roman times and studded with inscriptions from every empire that held it. From the ramparts the Tigris and the green Hevsel gardens open out below.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — the basalt radiates heat in summer
tip: Walk the stretch between Mardin Kapı and Yedi Kardeş bastion in the late afternoon for the Hevsel view; parts of the circuit are closed and it is not a continuous walk.
todo: Mardin Kapı to Yedi Kardeş rampart walk
The Tigris and Hevsel gardens view
rev: The scale impresses everyone, but access to the ramparts is patchy, some inner-city districts remain damaged and restricted since 2015–16, and it pays to ask locally which sections are open.
entry: Free · some bastions have a small fee
onward: Diyarbakır (DIY), 25 min into the old city by taxi

name: Diyarbakır Great Mosque
desc: The oldest mosque in Anatolia, built in 1091 on the frame of a Byzantine church and before that a temple, with recycled Roman columns and a courtyard that reads more like a Damascus mosque than a Turkish one.
tip: Sit in the courtyard for a while rather than going straight through — the two-storey arcades with their mismatched classical columns are the whole story of the city in one wall.
rev: Architecturally remarkable and free, though it is an active mosque with the usual timing and dress requirements, and the surrounding bazaar streets can feel chaotic.
entry: Free · closed to visitors during prayers
onward: Diyarbakır (DIY), 25 min to Sur; the mosque is in the middle of the walled city

name: Ten-Eyed Bridge
desc: A basalt bridge of 1065 carrying ten arches over the Tigris below the city walls, still standing on its original piers. Families picnic on the banks and the whole Hevsel garden belt spreads upstream.
tip: Come at sunset and walk it from the far bank looking back — the walls, the bridge and the river line up only from that side.
todo: Tea at a riverbank çay bahçesi
rev: A lovely free spot that locals clearly enjoy, though the riverbanks collect litter and the approach road from the old city is unpleasant on foot.
onward: Diyarbakır (DIY), 30 min by taxi below the southern walls

name: Zerzevan Castle
desc: A Roman garrison on the eastern frontier with a watchtower, rock-cut water channels, an underground church and — the reason it made headlines — an intact Mithraeum, one of the few in the world still bearing its cult niches.
tip: The Mithraeum is entered by a narrow stair and is often only opened on request; ask at the gate rather than assuming it is included.
rev: An excellent and still-quiet site that impresses almost everyone who makes the detour, though there is no shade, and excavation work regularly closes individual structures.
onward: Diyarbakır (DIY), then 45 min south by car on the Mardin road

name: Eğil
desc: A castle rock and Assyrian royal reliefs above a turquoise arm of the Tigris reservoir, with rock-cut tombs and prophets' shrines in the cliffs. The water colour against the bare stone is the surprise.
tip: Take the boat rather than only looking from the terrace — the cliff tombs and the reliefs only make sense from the water.
rev: Visitors are struck by the colour and the emptiness, though facilities are basic, boat schedules are informal, and the site is far less developed than photographs suggest.
entry: Free · boat trips around ₺250 (≈€5.50) per person
onward: Diyarbakır (DIY), then about 1h north by car

name: Çermik Travertines
desc: Terraces of white travertine built up by hot springs at Haydarhan, a smaller and almost unvisited cousin of Pamukkale, with thermal pools you can actually bathe in and no queue for anything.
season: Oct–May — the thermal water is best when the air is cold
tip: Go in winter, when steam rises off the terraces and the contrast with the cold air is the entire experience.
todo: A soak in the thermal pools
rev: Those who find it enjoy having a Pamukkale-like landscape to themselves, but the facilities are dated, the pools are basic, and the terraces are smaller than photos imply.
onward: Diyarbakır (DIY), then about 1h30 northwest by car

name: Hasankeyf
desc: A twelve-thousand-year-old town on the Tigris, most of it flooded by the Ilısu dam in 2020. The cave city and the castle rock survive above the waterline, and several monuments were cut up and moved to a new park on the hillside.
tip: Go knowing what it is now — the old bridge piers and the lower town are underwater, and the honest experience is the cave city plus the relocated monuments, not the town in the photographs.
todo: The cave city in the cliff face
Zeynel Bey tomb in the new park
The reservoir where the town stood
rev: Deeply mixed: some still find the setting extraordinary, many arrive expecting the pre-2020 town and leave saddened, and the relocated monuments in their landscaped park strike visitors as sterile.
entry: ₺100 (≈€2.20) for the castle and cave city
onward: Batman (BAL), then 45 min by car; minibuses run from Batman otogar

name: Malabadi Bridge
desc: An Artuqid bridge of 1147 whose single pointed arch spans nearly 40 metres over the Batman river — for centuries the widest stone arch in the world. Small chambers inside the abutments once sheltered travellers overnight.
tip: Pull off at the old road rather than the new highway bridge; from the riverbank below you get the arch reflected, which is the shot.
todo: The traveller chambers in the piers
The carved reliefs on the spandrels
rev: Engineering-minded visitors find the span genuinely impressive, though it is purely a roadside stop with no facilities and heavy traffic noise from the modern bridge alongside.
onward: Batman (BAL), then 45 min northwest by car on the Diyarbakır road

name: Hasuni Caves
desc: A rock-cut settlement of several hundred chambers, churches and water channels carved into a valley wall outside Batman, used from Roman times onward and only recently opened up with paths and lighting.
tip: Ask for the church with the carved cross and the baptismal basin — it is the best-preserved chamber and easy to miss on the marked route.
rev: An easy and rewarding side trip from Batman that few travellers know about, though interpretation is minimal and some chambers are gated off.
onward: Batman (BAL), then 30 min by car from the city

name: Tillo
desc: A hill village of scholars and mystics above Siirt, where a 17th-century astronomer built a tomb with a light channel that illuminates a specific point twice a year at the equinox. The stone lanes and the plain views are the rest of it.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the light event falls near the equinoxes
tip: If you can time it to 21 March or 23 September, the light beam through İbrahim Hakkı's tomb is the reason the village is known at all.
todo: İbrahim Hakkı tomb and its light channel
The view over the Siirt plain
rev: A quiet and genuinely unusual stop, but outside the equinox days there is not much to see, and visitors note the village is a pilgrimage site with a devotional rather than touristic atmosphere.
onward: Siirt (SXZ), then 25 min by car up from the city

name: Botan Valley
desc: A deep green canyon where the Botan river runs between limestone walls into the Tigris, now a national park with rafting in spring and swimming holes in summer. It is the wettest, greenest corner of a region people assume is all desert.
season: Apr–Jun for water, Sep–Oct for walking
tip: The Kasrik gorge stretch has the accessible viewpoints and picnic areas; the rest of the valley needs a boat or a guide.
near: Botan Vadisi Milli Parkı, Siirt, Türkiye
rev: A revelation for people who did not expect green canyons in the southeast, though infrastructure is thin, rafting operators are seasonal and informal, and roads into the valley are rough.
onward: Siirt (SXZ), then 40 min by car east toward the Kasrik gorge

name: Siirt Büryan and the Old Bazaar
desc: Lamb hung in a deep clay pit and cooked in its own steam overnight, served on flatbread in a handful of unchanged shops around Siirt's bazaar — a dish that basically does not exist outside this province and is eaten for breakfast.
season: Year-round — go early, they sell out by mid-morning
tip: Order büryan with perde pilavı alongside, and eat before ten; the good places cook one pit a day and close when it is gone.
todo: Siirt battaniye wool blankets in the bazaar
rev: Food travellers rate büryan among the best things they eat in Türkiye, with the caveat that the shops are plain, cash-only and crowded, and the fat content surprises people.
onward: Siirt (SXZ), 25 min into the city; the bazaar shops are walkable from the centre

name: Cizre and the Tigris
desc: An old Tigris crossing with an Artuqid bridge, the Ulu Camii and the tomb traditionally held to be Noah's, on a plain that has been a frontier for three thousand years under the wall of Cudi mountain.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — summer here is among the hottest in the country
tip: Check current travel advisories before planning this leg; conditions in Şırnak province change and local guidance is worth more than any guidebook.
todo: Noah's tomb in the old town
rev: Historically fascinating and almost never visited by foreigners, but this is a sensitive border area with checkpoints, and several governments advise against travel to parts of the province.
onward: Şırnak Şerafettin Elçi (NKT), then about 1h by car; check advisories before travelling

name: Mount Cudi
desc: A 2,100 m limestone massif above the Tigris that Islamic and local tradition names as the landing place of Noah's ark, with Assyrian rock reliefs on its lower slopes and villages that still summer on its pastures.
tip: This is not a casual hike — access depends on the security situation and permission, and it should only be attempted with local arrangement.
todo: Assyrian reliefs on the lower slopes
The Tigris plain from the ridge
rev: Of real interest to those drawn by the ark tradition, but access is frequently restricted, several governments advise against travel here, and independent hiking is not realistic.
entry: Free · access subject to local permission and security conditions
onward: Şırnak Şerafettin Elçi (NKT), then by road with local arrangement; check advisories first

name: Ravanda Castle
desc: A Crusader-era castle on a volcanic cone above the Kilis plain, its towers still legible and the view running south into Syria. Almost nobody comes, and the approach through olive groves is half the pleasure.
tip: The last stretch is a rough track — leave the car at the village and walk the final twenty minutes rather than risking the underside.
todo: The view south over the plain
rev: A satisfying ruin for people who like having a castle to themselves, though there is no signage, no facilities, and the border proximity means occasional checkpoints.
onward: Gaziantep (GZT), then about 1h15 by car via Kilis

name: Oylum Höyük
desc: One of the largest settlement mounds in the region, occupied more or less continuously from the Chalcolithic to the Iron Age, with a working excavation that has turned up Hittite and Mitanni layers. It is a mound rather than a monument, and reads as one.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov · dig season is summer
tip: Come during the summer dig season if you want it to mean anything — outside it there is little to see beyond the shape of the hill.
todo: The mound profile from the road
rev: Of genuine interest to archaeology travellers, but casual visitors report a bare hill with no interpretation, and access to trenches depends entirely on the dig team being present.
onward: Gaziantep (GZT), then about 1h by car to Kilis, then 15 min

name: Kilis Old Town and Kitchen
desc: A small border town with Ottoman stone houses, a good covered market and a cuisine that overlaps with Aleppo's — kilis tava, oruk, and a version of katmer worth the drive from Gaziantep on its own.
tip: Eat kilis tava at lunchtime in a market lokanta, then take the long way back to Antep through the olive country rather than the highway.
todo: Kilis tava in a market lokanta
Ottoman houses around the Ulu Camii
rev: Food-focused travellers find it a rewarding half-day from Gaziantep, though the town is otherwise quiet, hosts a large refugee population, and sits close enough to the border that some visitors feel uneasy.
onward: Gaziantep (GZT), then 1h by car south; frequent buses from Antep otogar

name: Sıra Gecesi in Urfa
desc: Urfa's traditional evening gathering: a stone courtyard, a sequence of long-drawn-out songs on bağlama and ney, çiğ köfte kneaded in front of you, and endless bitter coffee. It runs on its own logic and outsiders are usually folded in.
season: Year-round — most reliably on weekend evenings
tip: The konak restaurants near Balıklıgöl run scheduled versions for visitors; a real sıra gecesi is longer, later and only happens if someone invites you.
todo: Çiğ köfte kneaded at the table
rev: A genuine highlight for many visitors to Urfa, though the versions staged in restaurants can feel packaged, and the volume and length are not for everyone.
entry: Restaurant versions run about ₺500–800 (≈€11–18) with dinner
onward: Şanlıurfa GAP (GNY), 45 min to the centre; venues cluster near Balıklıgöl

name: Sof Mountain
desc: The pine ridge above Gaziantep where the city goes to escape the heat, with a small ski lift in winter, cool picnic terraces in summer and long views over the plain toward Syria.
season: Dec–Feb for snow, Jun–Sep as a heat escape
tip: Drive up in the evening in high summer — it is reliably ten degrees cooler than the city and the lights of Antep spread out below.
todo: The evening view over the city
The small ski lift in winter
rev: Locals value it highly as a break from the heat and it is free, but there is little for a visitor beyond the view, and the winter facilities are modest by any standard.
entry: Free · ski lift charged separately in season
onward: Gaziantep (GZT), then 40 min by car northwest of the city
